Apache Iceberg version: main (flink/v2.3) with the fix proposed for #18262 in #18288. On released versions, including 1.11.0, these cases already duplicate as part of #18262.
Query engine: Flink (DynamicIcebergSink, upsert and CDC modes)
Please describe the bug 🐞
Summary
#18262 describes the base bug. A schema change in the middle of a checkpoint splits a table across two writers. When the second writer updates a key that the first writer already wrote in that checkpoint, it produces an equality delete with the same sequence number as the first writer's row, so the delete never applies and both versions stay visible.
The fix proposed in #18288 lets all writers of a table share one inserted-row tracker for the length of a checkpoint. But writers can share only when their key types are compatible. In each case below the second writer still gets its own tracker, so the duplicate remains. Every case needs the same key to be written both before and after the change within one checkpoint.
Cases

An equality field becomes optional.

When it happens: when equality fields are set explicitly and aren't identifier fields (identifier fields must be required). EvolveSchemaVisitor makes a column optional when the input field is optional.
Why the obvious fix is unsafe: you can't simply ignore optionality when comparing key types. For a required int or long field, the comparator throws on null, and StructLikeWrapper.equals treats the exception as "not equal". So a tracker built for a required key never matches null keys, and null-key upserts through the new writer would duplicate.

An equality field's type is promoted (int → long, float → double, or decimal precision).

Why writers split: TableMetadataCache resolves records still on the old input schema to the old table schema. So a narrow writer and a wide writer can both be open, and records can alternate between them.
Why the tracker can't be shared as is: Integer and Long keys never match in a StructLikeMap. Negative values hash differently, and otherwise the comparison throws a ClassCastException that is swallowed as "not equal".

The equality-field set changes, through per-record DynamicRecord.setEqualityFields, or identifier fields changed outside the sink.

Why the tracker can't follow it: the tracker stores only key → position, so after any change one lookup direction is ambiguous. For example, after (id) → (id, tenant), an update for (7, B) projected back to id = 7 could retire tenant A's row.
Routing makes it worse: with key-hashed distribution, the old and new key of a row usually land on different subtasks anyway.

With a multi-column key, the key columns change order. EvolveSchemaVisitor can move columns to follow the input order, and the key type follows table column order. So a position-based key-type comparison doesn't match, and the writers don't share.

Expected behaviour
Either the writers share the tracker, so the later write retires the earlier row with a position delete; or, where sharing isn't possible, the sink makes the gap visible (a WARN and a metric) and the limitation is documented.
Possible directions (not yet evaluated upstream)

Case 1: build the tracker's map from an all-optional copy of the key type. Non-null keys compare exactly as before, and null matches null, as it does in an equality delete. Small and contained.
Case 2:

Same-scale decimal promotion keeps identical BigDecimal values, so it only needs the key-type check relaxed.
int → long and float → double need key conversion:

keep the first writer's key type as canonical
give writers of a promoted type a converting view
keep wide values that don't fit the narrow type in a separate map
normalise identity-partition keys the same way

The normal path stays unchanged.

Case 3: probably a documented limitation, plus a WARN and a metric when a second key set opens for the same table within a checkpoint.
Case 4: either compare key fields by field ID and reorder stored keys, or build the key projection in fi […]
title: Flink: DynamicIcebergSink still duplicates a row when a key column's optionality, type or order, or the equality-field set, changes within one checkpoint

Feature Request / Improvement
The table spec and the OpenAPI spec disagree on how binary and fixed values are written as hex strings:

format/spec.md, Appendix D (JSON single-value serialization): "Stored as a hexadecimal string", with the example "000102ff" (lowercase), and no case rule.
rest-catalog-open-api.yaml, BinaryTypeValue / FixedTypeValue: "serialized as an uppercase hexadecimal string".

Implementations differ:

Java's SingleValueParser writes uppercase (Guava base16()) and reads case-insensitively, upper-casing the input before decoding.
iceberg-go writes lowercase for binary/fixed defaults in table metadata (initial-default / write-default), and uppercase for expression literals.

So both cases can already appear in table metadata.
Proposal:

Readers must accept either case. Lowercase values can already be written by existing implementations, so a stricter rule would break existing tables.
Writers should emit uppercase, matching the OpenAPI schema and the reference implementation.
Update the Appendix D example to uppercase ("000102FF"), and add the reader rule to the OpenAPI descriptions.

Happy to open a PR once there's agreement.

Apache Iceberg version: 1.11.0 (reproduced). On main, the class check in PartitionData.get(pos, javaClass) is the same and PartitionSummary and SnapshotSummary are unchanged; I have not run the repro on main.
Query engine: None (core API). The same failure shows up when a Flink DynamicIcebergSink checkpoint spans the promotion.
Please describe the bug 🐞
Summary
UpdateSchema.updateColumn allows int → long and float → double on a column that is the source of an identity partition field (truncate on int / long should behave the same; I did not test it). The partition spec keeps its ID, and TableMetadata rebinds it to the new schema, so its partition type becomes long (or double). PartitionData.get(pos, javaClass) then rejects a value of the other class. As a result:

A data file built before the promotion, whose partition holds an Integer, cannot be committed after it.
A data file built after the promotion cannot be added to a manifest written with a PartitionSpec obtained before the promotion.
One commit that contains files from both sides fails in either case. A Flink dynamic sink checkpoint that spans the promotion produces exactly that.

It surfaced while looking at the non-key partition cases of #18350.
Steps to reproduce
Schema schema = new Schema(
    Types.NestedField.required(1, "id", Types.IntegerType.get()),
    Types.NestedField.optional(2, "region", Types.IntegerType.get()));
PartitionSpec spec = PartitionSpec.builderFor(schema).identity("region").build();
Table table = /* any catalog */ createTable(schema, spec);
PartitionSpec specBeforePromotion = table.spec();

PartitionData partition = new PartitionData(table.spec().partitionType());
partition.set(0, 5); // Integer, built before the promotion
DataFile before = DataFiles.builder(table.spec())
    .withPath("/before.parquet")
    .withFileSizeInBytes(10)
    .withRecordCount(1)
    .withPartition(partition)
    .build();

table.updateSchema().updateColumn("region", Types.LongType.get()).commit();

table.newAppend().appendFile(before).commit(); // case 1
For case 2, build a file the same way after the promotion with the partition value 5L, and add it to a manifest created with ManifestFiles.write(2, specBeforePromotion, outputFile, 1L).
Control: the 5L file built after the promotion, appended to the table with the current spec, commits fine.
Expected behavior
Both files commit. A partition value written before the promotion is accepted for the promoted partition type, and a file with a promoted partition value can be written to a manifest from an older bound spec of the same spec ID.
Actual behavior
Case 1, from SnapshotSummary.Builder.updatePartitions → PartitionSpec.partitionToPath → PartitionData.get:
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Wrong class, expected java.lang.Long, but was java.lang.Integer, for object: 5

Case 2, from ManifestWriter.addEntry → PartitionSummary.updateFields:
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Wrong class, expected java.lang.Integer, but was java.lang.Long, for object: 5

Case 3, in a Flink dynamic sink checkpoint with files from both sides: the same two messages, depending on which spec object is used. I reproduced this only by passing both kinds of files through the sink's manifest utilities and a RowDelta in a test, not in a running job. All 5 variants I tried failed, including 3 controls with no re-write at all.
Notes

Likely impact in Flink DynamicIcebergSink: DynamicWriteResultAggregator caches table.specs() per table and looks specs up by ID, which the promotion keeps. An aggregator that saw the table before the promotion would then fail on the first post-promotion checkpoint, even with one writer. I inferred this from reading the code; I did not run a job.
Bucket partitions are not affected: their values are Integer at both widths.
float → double on an identity partition column fails the same way in a sink test.
I haven't worked out the fix. Options to discuss: make PartitionData accept the narrower numeric class for a promoted t […]

body:
Apache Iceberg version
main (development)
Query engine
Other
Please describe the bug 🐞
DateTimeUtil.convertMicros and DateTimeUtil.convertNanos return the previous unit for a pre-epoch timestamp in the first second of a unit when its fraction is .999999 (.999999999 for nanos). This affects the year, month, day and hour transforms.
var day = Transforms.day().bind(Types.TimestampType.withoutZone());
long midnight = -86_400_000_000L; // 1969-12-31T00:00:00
day.apply(midnight + 999_998);    // -1
day.apply(midnight + 999_999);    // -2, expected -1
day.apply(midnight + 1_000_000);  // -1
The spec defines day as days from 1970-01-01, so 1969-12-31T00:00:00.999999 should be -1. The transform also stops being monotonic, which inclusive projection relies on, so Java's own scan skips a matching row:
// row 1969-12-31T00:00:00.999999 is written to partition ts_day = -2
Projections.inclusive(spec).project(greaterThanOrEqual("ts", midnight + 500_000));
// -> ts_day >= -1, so the file holding the row is pruned
Likelihood: low. It needs a pre-epoch timestamp, in the first second of an hour/day/month/year, with a fraction of exactly .999999 (.999999999 for nanos). Second- or millisecond-precision data never hits it. For random microsecond-precision pre-epoch values it's roughly 1 in 10^11 rows for day and 1 in 4×10^9 for hour.
Cause: the negative branch adds 1 to the fraction but not to the seconds:
long epochSecond = Math.floorDiv(micros, MICROS_PER_SECOND);
long nanoAdjustment = Math.floorMod(micros + 1, MICROS_PER_SECOND) * 1000;
At .999999, micros + 1 crosses into the next second but epochSecond does not, so the timestamp lands almost a second earlier. In the first second of a unit, that crosses into the previous unit.
Fix: Math.floorDiv(micros + 1, MICROS_PER_SECOND), and the same in convertNanos with NANOS_PER_SECOND. I checked the micros version against floor semantics for year, month, day and hour across ~47k values, including every unit boundary from 1900 to 1971: the current code is wrong for 3,446 of them, the fix for none.
iceberg-rust returns the calendar day for these values, see the iceberg-rust day transform fix.
Related: #18115 (same class of bug, rounding toward zero instead of down for pre-epoch values, but in microsecond conversion rather than the transforms), #9714 (transform rounding for negative values isn't specified). The +1/-1 adjustment comes from #1981.
Willingness to contribute

 I would be willing to contribute a fix for this bug with guidance from the Iceberg community
 I cannot contribute a fix for this bug at this time
title: Temporal transforms put pre-epoch timestamps at `.999999` into the previous unit

Apache Iceberg version
1.11.0 (also present on main today: core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/rest/auth/AuthSessionCache.java L54-58, OAuth2Manager.java L216-217, util/ThreadPools.java L101-104)
Query engine
Spark 4.1.1, as a long-lived Spark Connect server (many short-lived sessions on one driver JVM), REST catalog with the default oauth2 auth (Apache Polaris).
Please describe the bug 🐞
OAuth2Manager.newSessionCache creates its AuthSessionCache through the public constructor, which builds a dedicated single-thread pool with ThreadPools.newExitingWorkerPool(name + "-auth-session-evict", 1). That goes through Guava's MoreExecutors.getExitingExecutorService, which registers a JVM shutdown hook (Runtime.addShutdownHook(new Thread(...))) that is never removed. AuthSessionCache.close() shuts the executor down but the hook stays registered.
On a long-lived JVM that creates many catalog instances (Spark creates one catalog plugin, hence one OAuth2Manager, per Spark session) this has two effects:

java.lang.ApplicationShutdownHooks.hooks grows by one unstarted Thread per catalog instance for the life of the JVM.
Each hook Thread is constructed on the calling thread, so it copies that thread's inheritable thread-locals. Spark's SparkSession.activeThreadSession is an InheritableThreadLocal, so every hook pins the Spark session that created the catalog, including sessions that have since been closed, together with their catalogs, table caches and every loaded TableMetadata (full snapshot history). Heap dump, Eclipse MAT, GC-root path with weak/soft references excluded (it is the only path):

java.lang.ApplicationShutdownHooks.hooks
 └ Thread "DelayedShutdownHook-for-java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor@…"   (never started)
    └ inheritableThreadLocals → ThreadLocalMap → Entry.value
       └ org.apache.spark.sql.classic.SparkSession   (a CLOSED Spark Connect session, ~36 MB retained)

Measured on a shared Spark Connect driver (4 GiB heap): 319 such hook threads after ~3 h; ApplicationShutdownHooks retained 51% of the live heap; releasing or idle-expiring sessions returned 0-9% of it; the heap left after each full GC only grew until the driver ran out of memory, roughly daily.
The same pattern (a per-call exiting pool, hence a hook per call) exists in RewriteDataFilesSparkAction.rewriteService() (Rewrite-Service: 296 hooks after one rewrite_data_files sweep), RewritePositionDeleteFilesSparkAction.rewriteService() and BaseProcedure.executorService(...) when a pool size is passed.
#15031 covers the hooks of the static pools in ThreadPools (class-loader leaks on hot reload). This report is about the per-instance and per-call pools, whose hooks multiply with the number of catalogs and calls.
To reproduce: on one JVM, create N OAuth2Manager instances (for example N Spark Connect sessions that each read from a REST catalog with OAuth2), close them, force a full GC, then look at java.lang.ApplicationShutdownHooks.hooks (N new entries) or a live heap histogram (the N closed SparkSession objects are still reachable).
Suggested fix: per-instance and per-call caches should not use an "exiting" pool. Options:

(a) one shared static daemon evictor for all AuthSessionCache instances, passed as a plain Executor so close() does not shut it down, with its thread created with inheritable thread-locals disabled (new Thread(null, r, name, 0, false)) so even that single thread pins nothing;
(b) a plain daemon pool that close() shuts down, with no shutdown hook;
(c) if a hook is kept, remove it in close() and construct the hook thread with inherited thread-locals disabled.

We run (a) in production as an OAuth2Manager subclass loaded through rest.auth.type=<fqcn> (overriding newSessionCache and using the package-private AuthSessionCache(Duration, Executor, Ticker) constructor): closed sessions are collected at the next GC and the heap floor returns.
Willingness to contribute

 I would be willing to contribute a fix for this bug with guidance from the Ice […]
title: Core: AuthSessionCache's exiting evictor pool registers a never-removed JVM shutdown hook per OAuth2Manager, pinning the creating thread's inheritable thread-locals (leaks closed Spark sessions)

Feature Request / Improvement
Spark 4.2 introduces the DSv2 Transaction API (org.apache.spark.sql.connector.catalog.TransactionalCatalogPlugin, org.apache.spark.sql.connector.catalog.transactions.{Transaction, TransactionInfo}, all @since 4.2.0). This sub-issue tracks implementing it in the Iceberg Spark connector, as listed in the Spark 4.2 feature tracker #17959.
Proposed scope

Implement TransactionalCatalogPlugin in the Spark catalog(s) so beginTransaction(TransactionInfo) returns an Iceberg-backed Transaction.
Wire the transaction lifecycle to Iceberg core's Transaction API: stage writes under the transaction, commit() commits them, abort() discards staged changes (idempotent), close() releases resources (idempotent).
Track the read set for conflict resolution at commit time; implement registerScans(Scan[]) so Spark can offer materialized scans (cache reuse) for registration against the transaction.
Decide transaction granularity (catalog-level transaction with per-table staged writes) and document interaction with existing write paths (SupportsAtomicV2Writes, row-level operations) and Iceberg snapshot-isolation semantics.

Open design questions (for discussion before implementation)

Which SQL statements trigger transactional execution, and how do mixed transactional/non-transactional writes behave?
Conflict detection/resolution at commit time vs. delegating to Iceberg's existing snapshot-conflict checks.
Whether SparkCatalog, SparkSessionCatalog, or both should implement the interface.

Part of #17959.

Apache Iceberg version
1.11.0. That release includes MaxCommittedCheckpointIdValidator from #14517 (ported to flink/v2.0 in #14637), and the bug is in how that validator interacts with the commit retry loop. The build we ran also cherry-picks #16648 into DynamicCommitter. It does not touch the validator, commitOperation, the retry or the cleanup. All lines cited below are from the stock apache-iceberg-1.11.0 tag.
Query engine
Flink (DynamicIcebergSink / DynamicCommitter, flink/v2.0), REST catalog
Please describe the bug 🐞
A REST catalog applied a RowDelta commit from DynamicCommitter, but the client got a 409 back for the same commit. On the retry, MaxCommittedCheckpointIdValidator (added in #14517) found the checkpoint already on main and threw MaxCommittedCheckpointMismatchException. That exception extends ValidationException, which implements CleanableFailure, so SnapshotProducer.commit() ran cleanAll(). cleanAll() deleted the manifest list and the new data manifest of the snapshot the catalog had already made current.
DynamicCommitter then caught the exception and logged Skipping commit operation rowDelta ... already contains changes for checkpoint N. The table was left with a current snapshot whose manifest list returned 404. Every later commit and committer restore failed with NoSuchKey until the two objects were restored from S3 object versions.
Observed sequence (single writer, no other snapshot between S(n-1) and S(n+1), no compaction in the window):

Spark
Please describe the bug 🐞
Spark 4.0. With 1.12.0 (#16292, vectorized Parquet reads for variant columns), any vectorized Spark read of a data file that contains a shredded VARIANT column fails if the query doesn't project that column. Vectorization is on by default, so a table written with write.parquet.shred-variants=true can no longer serve queries that select only its non-variant columns. Queries that do select the variant work, because they fall back to row reads.
Repro (Spark 4.0, Hadoop catalog):
CREATE TABLE db.t (id BIGINT, v VARIANT) USING iceberg
  TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version'='3', 'write.parquet.shred-variants'='true');
INSERT INTO db.t
  SELECT id, parse_json(concat('{"a":', id, ',"b":"x', id, '"}')) FROM range(1000);

SELECT sum(variant_get(v, '$.a', 'int')) FROM db.t;  -- OK (row-based read)
SELECT sum(id) FROM db.t;                            -- fails
SET spark.sql.iceberg.vectorization.enabled=false;
SELECT sum(id) FROM db.t;                            -- OK
java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: Unsupported variant: shredded typed_value primitive
  at org.apache.iceberg.arrow.vectorized.VectorizedVariantVisitor.primitive(VectorizedVariantVisitor.java:97)
  at org.apache.iceberg.parquet.ParquetVariantVisitor.visitValue(ParquetVariantVisitor.java:207)
  at org.apache.iceberg.parquet.ParquetVariantVisitor.visitObjectFields(ParquetVariantVisitor.java:259)
  at org.apache.iceberg.parquet.ParquetVariantVisitor.visit(ParquetVariantVisitor.java:177)
  at org.apache.iceberg.parquet.TypeWithSchemaVisitor.visitVariant(TypeWithSchemaVisitor.java:218)
  at org.apache.iceberg.parquet.TypeWithSchemaVisitor.visitFields(TypeWithSchemaVisitor.java:208)
  at org.apache.iceberg.spark.data.vectorized.VectorizedSparkParquetReaders.buildReader(VectorizedSparkParquetReaders.java:61)
  at org.apache.iceberg.spark.source.BatchDataReader.open(BatchDataReader.java:128)

Analysis. The shredded-file fallback in #16292 only covers projected variants:

SparkBatch.useParquetBatchReads() / supportsParquetBatchReads(...) check expectedSchema.columns(). A projected variant on a shredded table (by table property, or variant lower bounds in the file) disables batch reads. An unprojected variant is never considered, so batch reads are chosen.
VectorizedSparkParquetReaders.buildReader then visits the file schema with TypeWithSchemaVisitor. For the unprojected variant group, visitVariant is reached with iType == null, but it still calls ParquetVariantVisitor.visit(variantGroup, visitor.variantVisitor()).
VectorizedVariantVisitor throws on the shredded typed_value (primitive(...), and value(...) when typedResult != null) before anything checks whether the column is projected. findVariantField would return null for it anyway.

Spark 4.1 / 4.2 on main appear to share the same SparkBatch logic and reader path, but I've only reproduced on 4.0.
Related: #17736 (closed) proposed routing all projected variants to the row reader because plan-time shredding detection isn't sound, and noted that queries not projecting a variant "are unaffected and still vectorize". This issue is that unprojected case: it isn't unaffected, because the reader builder still walks the unprojected shredded group. #18121 (open) reworks the same SparkBatch check but still only over projected variants.
Possible fix: skip the variant sub-visit when the column isn't projected. Either have TypeWithSchemaVisitor.visitVariant call visitor.variant(null, group, null) when variant == null, or have VectorizedReaderBuilder return no variant visitor for unprojected columns. Either way the unprojected column is ignored, the same as for unprojected primitives.
Workarounds: project the variant (forces a row read), or disable vectorization (spark.sql.iceberg.vectorization.enabled=false, or the vectorization-enabled=false read option), at the cost of all vectorized reads on that scan.

Actual

The converter runs one cycle and the lock is released (Received lock released event).
RewriteDataFiles [0] then runs and finishes: LockRemoverOperator logs Processing result ... RewriteDataFiles [0]. No Received lock released event follows.
From then on, TriggerManagerOperator logs Failed to acquire lock. Delaying task to ... on every check (21 times in a 120s run, 33 in a 180s run), and concurrentRunThrottled keeps growing.
Neither task runs again. processedStagingSnapshotNum stays at 0, and equality-delete files pile up: 48 after 120s, 96 after 180s.
With the converter as the only maintenance task, the same table and load ran normally in five runs: 31 conversion commits, no errors.

Cause, as far as we can tell

Every task's pipeline sees every trigger's watermark. Filter <i> (TableMaintenance.java:329-337) drops other tasks' records but not their watermarks. All task outputs are unioned into Lock remover (:349-365).

Apache Iceberg version: 1.12.0 (reproduced). The code involved appears unchanged on main (flink/v2.3), so the same behaviour is expected there.
Query engine: Flink (DynamicIcebergSink, DataStream API, upsert mode)
Please describe the bug 🐞
Summary
DynamicIcebergSink.TableMetadataCache.schema() iterates all historical schemas of a table by schema id ascending and returns the first one that CompareSchemasVisitor marks SAME with the input. The visitor compares by field name (via PartnerIdByNameAccessors) and does not consider the input's field ids, so when a dropped column is reused — the typical case is DROP COLUMN c → ADD COLUMN c <same type> — the matcher picks the historical schema that still holds the retired field id. The writer then writes the Parquet file against the retired id, and the reader with the current schema cannot locate the field and returns null (or initial-default on tables with that feature).
The same name-first matching also masks changes that would otherwise trigger the sink's auto schema evolution:

DROP COLUMN c followed by inputs that happen to match an older schema that still contained c → dropUnusedColumns(true) never fires, the column stays in the current schema.
DROP COLUMN c → ADD COLUMN c with the sink's auto schema evolution path → SCHEMA_UPDATE_NEEDED is never returned, so the sink never issues addColumn, and the column is not re-added to the catalog.

Root cause
Line numbers at tag apache-iceberg-1.12.0, flink/v2.2.

TableMetadataCache#schema(TableIdentifier, Schema, boolean) iterates cached.tableSchemas.entrySet() (= table.schemas(), every historical schema sorted by schema id ascending) and returns the first entry whose CompareSchemasVisitor.visit(input, tableSchema, ...) is SAME (TableMetadataCache.java:140-184).
CompareSchemasVisitor resolves the partner on the table side with PartnerIdByNameAccessors, so matching is name-based; the field() method only checks name/type/optionality and does not require the input's field id to match the table's (CompareSchemasVisitor.java).
After DROP COLUMN c → ADD COLUMN c the current schema (schema id N) has c with a new field id, but schema id N-1 (or any earlier schema that contained c with the retired field id) is still in table.schemas(). The historical schema is iterated first and returned as SAME.
ResolvedSchemaInfo is built from that historical schema, so the writer serializes the Parquet file using the retired field id. Readers consulting the current schema look up the new field id, do not find it in the file, and return null.

The per-input-schema cache (cached.inputSchemas) also returns the stale ResolvedSchemaInfo directly on subsequent writes of the same input shape, bypassing the TTL check (TableMetadataCache.java:141-146), so a short cacheRefreshMs does not help.
Reproduction
Minimal DataStream job against an Iceberg table (REST catalog, upsert mode, equality field id):
// schema v0:  (id INT PK, val STRING)
// schema v1:  v0 + (c STRING)   -- addColumn("c", STRING)
// schema v2:  deleteColumn("c")
// schema v3:  addColumn("c", STRING)  -- same name, same type

body:
Apache Iceberg version
1.12.0 (latest release)
Query engine
Spark
Please describe the bug 🐞
SparkBatch.equals compares the table name and the hash code of the scan that created the batch, so the batches of two scans whose hash codes collide are equal even when the scans read different data. Spark's BatchScanExec.equals compares batches and exchange reuse relies on it, so Spark reuses one scan's shuffle for the other and returns its rows for both.
Reproduction in plain Spark SQL with default settings:
CREATE TABLE t (id BIGINT, data STRING) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (data);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'Aa'), (2, 'BB');

SELECT sum(id) FROM t WHERE data = 'Aa'
UNION ALL
SELECT sum(id) FROM t WHERE data = 'BB';
This returns 1 and 1 instead of 1 and 2. 'Aa' and 'BB' have the same String.hashCode(), so the two scans' filter descriptions, and with them the scans, hash alike. The filters select whole identity partitions, so Iceberg evaluates them completely and no Spark Filter above the scans tells the branches apart. The final plan (Spark 4.2, main) reuses the first branch's exchange for the second:
Union
:- HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[sum(id#12L)], output=[sum(id)#18L])
:  +- ShuffleQueryStage 0
:     +- Exchange SinglePartition, ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS, [plan_id=91]
:        +- *(1) HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[partial_sum(id#12L)], output=[sum#38L])
:           +- *(1) Project [id#12L]
:              +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
:                 +- BatchScan testhadoop.default.table[id#12L, data#13] IcebergScan(table=testhadoop.default.table, schemaId=0, snapshotId=369853115188610976, branch=null, filters=data IS NOT NULL, data = 'Aa', runtimeFilters=, groupedBy=) RuntimeFilters: []
+- HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[sum(id#14L)], output=[sum(id)#19L])
   +- ShuffleQueryStage 2
      +- ReusedExchange [sum#39L], Exchange SinglePartition, ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS, [plan_id=91]

The scans' own equals methods compare their table, snapshot, read schema and filters; SparkScan.toBatch() and SparkChangelogScan.toBatch() pass only hashCode() to SparkBatch (since #5934), in every Spark module. Any two scans of the same table whose 32-bit hash codes collide are affected when the plans above them match, and string literals with equal hash codes, like 'Aa' and 'BB', make the collision deterministic. #13437 proposed a stronger digest for this but was closed as stale.

Feature Request / Improvement
Data Processing Context
One of my major data pipeline relies on Iceberg's MERGE INTO, where the table is partitioned on multiple partition keys. For example, the partition keys are date and bucket(N, id). Each new data slice that lands on a new date might also exist in the target table in a different date, and the pipeline need to deduplicate via MERGE INTO with id as the only join key.
Considering shuffle is the biggest bottleneck on the performance, I'd like to start adopting SPJ, allowing SPJ on subset of partition keys. However, with preserve-data-grouping enabled, Spark will load all files that make up the same bucket into a single executor, which will cause OOM.
The most obvious solution to me seems require increasing the granularity of the second partition key, e.g. from bucket(N, id) to bucket(N*m, id), that will reduce the data loaded to each executor by a factor of m, increasing parallelism by a factor of m. However, it will also increase the file count by the same factor, and it will introduce new problems related to small files.
Improvement Idea
My first question would be: are there any established pattern/strategy to solve the problem without suffering from small file problem? I can only think about adjusting the partition layout, e.g. from date & bucket(N, id) into week(date) & bucket(N*m, id), increasing the files by a factor of only m/7. It can also involves further pruning, such as month(date) instead of week to change it into m/30.
Another idea is to enable node-local shuffle. Instead of pure SPJ, Spark might still do limited shuffle as long as all rows that belong to the same bucket/partition group are loaded into the same node, and shuffle are done purely on node-level without triggering cluster-wide shuffles.

Apache Iceberg version
main (e70a2efcd)
Query engine
Spark 4.2. The same NOT_EQ and NOT conversion paths exist in the Spark 3.5, 4.0 and 4.1 source directories, but I haven't run the reproduction on those versions.
Please describe the bug 🐞
DELETE FROM t WHERE data <> 'a1' can also delete rows where data is NULL, although SELECT ... WHERE data <> 'a1' doesn't return them. In SQL NULL <> 'a1' is NULL, so those rows should stay.
Iceberg's notEqual against a non-null literal and notStartsWith match null values, unlike the corresponding SQL predicates. SparkV2Filters explicitly adds notNull for supported NOT IN predicates ("col NOT IN (1, 2) in Spark is equal to notNull(col) && notIn(col, 1, 2) in Iceberg"), but its NOT_EQ path calls handleNotEqual without that guard, and its generic NOT path negates the converted child.
If SparkTable.canDeleteUsingMetadata accepts the resulting expression, deleteWhere passes it to deleteFromRowFilter, and files containing NULL rows can be deleted. Single-value NOT IN ('a1') shows the same result as <>; an optimizer rewrite to an equality may explain this, but I haven't captured the pushed predicate to confirm it.
Reproduction
A TestDeleteFrom-style test in spark/v4.2, run with the Hadoop catalog. spark_catalog, Hive and REST gave the same results for NOT LIKE and single-value NOT IN; the other rows were run with the Hadoop catalog only.
Each predicate runs against a freshly created table, once partitioned and once unpartitioned ([PARTITIONED BY (data)] is an optional clause, not literal SQL):
CREATE TABLE t (id bigint, data string) USING iceberg [PARTITIONED BY (data)] TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version'='2');
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'a1'), (2, 'b'), (3, CAST(NULL AS STRING));
SELECT id FROM t WHERE <predicate>;   -- returns 2 in every case below
DELETE FROM t WHERE <predicate>;
SELECT id FROM t;
In this setup the insert wrote three data files for the partitioned table and two for the unpartitioned one; the unpartitioned result may depend on the file layout and on whether a metadata-only delete is possible.
Rows left after the DELETE (expected: 1, 3):

predicate
unpartitioned
PARTITIONED BY (data)

data <> 'a1'
1
1

data NOT IN ('a1')
1
1

data NOT LIKE 'a%'
1
fails with the ResidualEvaluator NPE from #18412

data NOT IN ('a1', 'x')
1, 3
1, 3

The deletes that removed id 3 committed delete snapshots. The two-value NOT IN control kept id 3 (a delete snapshot for the partitioned table, overwrite for the unpartitioned one).
With the ResidualEvaluator change from #18414 applied, the partitioned NOT LIKE case no longer throws and also leaves only id 1 in a delete snapshot. #18590 contains the same production change.
Possible fix
The expression used for a metadata-only DELETE has to match exactly the rows SQL matches, including for NULL. For the cases above that means excluding NULL for <> and for negated STARTS_WITH. This can't be a blanket notNull for every single-column NOT, since predicates such as NOT (data IS NOT NULL) or a negated null-safe equality do match NULL, and nested or compound predicates need to keep their SQL semantics too. Would it be better to make the conversion exact for these cases, or to skip metadata-only deletion when an exact conversion isn't guaranteed and fall back to the row-level path?

Apache Iceberg version
main (development)
Query engine
None
Please describe the bug 🐞
With a local warehouse (warehouse="file://...", PyArrowFileIO with PyArrowLocalFileSystem), PyIceberg writes
every new file (Parquet data files, *-m0.avro manifests, snap-*.avro manifest lists, NNNNN-<uuid>.metadata.json)
through pyarrow.fs.LocalFileSystem.open_output_stream() and closes it, but never calls fsync on any of them or on
their directories. It then swaps the catalog pointer to the new metadata.json. The catalog backend syncs its own
commit (SQLite: fdatasync of the journal, the directory and the database file), and that commit also forces the
ext4 journal, which makes the creation of the new files durable while their contents are still only in the page
cache.
After a power loss (or kernel crash) shortly after an acknowledged commit, every file PyIceberg wrote is present
but 0 bytes, and the catalog points to a 0-byte metadata.json:
pyiceberg.catalog.load_table("ns.t")
  ValidationError: 1 validation error for TableMetadataWrapper
  Invalid JSON: EOF while parsing a value at line 1 column 0 [type=json_invalid, input_value='', input_type=str]

So one commit makes the whole table unloadable, including every earlier snapshot, because the table is opened
only through the newest metadata file and the older metadata files are just as empty. There is no supported way
to fall back. A plain process kill (no power loss) is always fine, because the page cache survives.
With the SQLite catalog there is a second, smaller effect: SQLite's default rollback journal (journal_mode=DELETE,
synchronous=FULL) commits by unlinking catalog.db-journal without syncing the directory, so after the power
loss the hot journal rolls back the most recent catalog transaction. The catalog then points to the previous
metadata.json (also 0 bytes), and a table created just before the cut disappears from the catalog. That part
would be fixed by PRAGMA synchronous=EXTRA (or WAL mode) on the SQLite connection. The main problem, the
unsynced warehouse files, is independent of the catalog: with a PostgreSQL catalog (on another disk) and a local warehouse
the new pointer survives the cut and points to a metadata.json that is either missing (cut before ext4's next
journal commit: FileNotFoundError) or 0 bytes (cut after it: the same ValidationError).

schema = pa.schema([("id", pa.int64()), ("v", pa.string())])
t = cat.create_table("ns.t", schema=schema)
print("ACK create_table ns.t", flush=True)
for i in range(n):
    lo = i * 100
    t.append(pa.table({"id": list(range(lo, lo + 100)), "v": [f"r{j}" for j in range(lo, lo + 100)]}, schema=schema))
    print(f"ACK append {lo}..{lo + 100}", flush=True)

body:
Problem / Motivation
The Configuration page documents three isolation-level table properties:

write.delete.isolation-level
write.update.isolation-level
write.merge.isolation-level

There is no explicit note that these properties are scoped only to row-level operations
(DELETE, UPDATE, MERGE) and have no effect on append/INSERT operations. As a result, users
reasonably assume that setting one of these properties can reduce commit conflicts or commit
duration for append-heavy workloads. This is a common source of misunderstanding when
diagnosing 409 CommitFailedException responses from a REST catalog.
Real-world scenario that motivated this request
We run 5 Iceberg tables, each written by ~30 independent Flink append jobs with a 1-minute
checkpoint interval (≈27 commits/minute per table), committed through a REST catalog
(Lakekeeper). We observed frequent 409 responses from the catalog (CommitFailedException,
assert-ref-snapshot-id not satisfied), with commit retries.
Our team set write.delete.isolation-level = snapshot on these tables, expecting it to reduce
commit conflicts or commit duration. It had no effect on the append path, because:

The Flink append path commits via AppendFiles (table.newAppend()), which does not
invoke validateNoConflictingData or any data-conflict validation.
The write.*.isolation-level properties are read by Spark's DELETE / UPDATE / MERGE paths,
not by append.
A 409 from the REST catalog is a metadata-pointer conflict, resolved by retry regardless
of isolation level (see the "Concurrent write operations" / "Retry validation" sections on
the Reliability page).

Proposed change
Add an explicit note to the documentation stating that:

write.delete.isolation-level, write.update.isolation-level, and write.merge.isolation-level
apply only to row-level operations (DELETE, UPDATE, MERGE).
Append/INSERT has no isolation level; concurrent append conflicts are resolved at the
metadata level via retry, and there is no data-conflict check to configure.

Suggested locations (either or both):

Configuration page → Write properties section, next to the three isolation-level rows.
Reliability page → "Concurrent write operations" / "Retry validation" subsection, as a
short cross-reference clarifying that retry-based conflict resolution applies to append.

Additional context

Iceberg versions in use: 1.8.x (Spark maintenance) and 1.11.0 (Flink 2.1.2, iceberg-flink-runtime-2.1).
Catalog: REST (Lakekeeper), S3 storage with remote signing.
The confusion is not about a missing feature — it is about the docs not making the
append/row-level scoping of the write.*.isolation-level properties explicit.
title: Clarify that write.*.isolation-level properties do not apply to append/INSERT

Summary
The Flink ConvertEqualityDeletes maintenance task (added in 1.12.0) fails on every conversion cycle when the equality field columns include a DATE column. No cycle ever commits. Because the converter requires the partition source columns to be part of the equality fields, this affects any table partitioned by a date column, which is a very common layout for CDC and log tables.
Environment

iceberg-flink-runtime-1.20-1.12.0.jar
Flink 1.20.0
Format version 3 table, Parquet data files
Writer: Flink upsert sink writing to a staging branch
Converter: a separate Flink job running TableMaintenance + ConvertEqualityDeletes with stagingBranch("staging") and targetBranch("main")

Steps to reproduce

Create a v3 table:
CREATE TABLE t (
  id BIGINT,
  d  DATE,
  v  STRING,
  PRIMARY KEY (id, d) NOT ENFORCED
) PARTITIONED BY (d)
WITH ('format-version' = '3', 'write.upsert.enabled' = 'true');

With Flink, write to the staging branch: insert a row, then update the same key, so that equality delete files are produced. The same failure also happens with write.upsert.enabled=false (changelog input with -U/+U).

Start the converter:
TableMaintenance.forTable(env, tableLoader)
    .add(
        ConvertEqualityDeletes.builder()
            .stagingBranch("staging")
            .targetBranch("main")
            .equalityFieldColumns(List.of("id", "d"))
            .scheduleOnInterval(Duration.ofSeconds(60)))
    .append();

Equality deletes on staging are resolved to deletion vectors and committed to main.

Every cycle fails in EqualityConvertReader. The committer logs Skipping commit ... a DV writer reported an error and the TaskResult has success=false:
java.lang.ClassCastException: class java.time.LocalDate cannot be cast to class java.lang.Integer (java.time.LocalDate and java.lang.Integer are in module java.base of loader 'bootstrap')
	at org.apache.iceberg.types.Conversions.toByteBuffer(Conversions.java:100)
	at org.apache.iceberg.types.Conversions.toByteBuffer(Conversions.java:87)
	at org.apache.iceberg.flink.maintenance.operator.StructLikeSerializer.writeField(StructLikeSerializer.java:135)
	at org.apache.iceberg.flink.maintenance.operator.StructLikeSerializer.serializeKey(StructLikeSerializer.java:63)
	at org.apache.iceberg.flink.maintenance.operator.EqualityConvertReader.processDataFile(EqualityConvertReader.java:168)
	at org.apache.iceberg.flink.maintenance.operator.EqualityConvertReader.processElement(EqualityConvertReader.java:115)

All references are to the apache-iceberg-1.12.0 tag, flink/v1.20:

Apache Iceberg version
1.12.0 (iceberg-spark-runtime-4.1_2.13, Spark 4.1.3)
Query engine
Spark (also affects any engine that loads equality deletes through BaseDeleteLoader with the generic Parquet reader)
Please describe the bug
An equality delete file keyed on a fixed(L) column deletes almost nothing on read: N distinct keys behave like a single key.
Repro

v2 table (id long, f fixed(4)), write.delete.mode=merge-on-read; insert 1000 rows with a distinct f per row (e.g. the 4 big-endian bytes of id).
Write one Parquet equality delete file on f with 143 distinct keys (id = 0, 7, 14, ..., 994) using GenericFileWriterFactory (or SparkFileWriterFactory), commit it with newRowDelta().addDeletes(...).
SELECT id FROM t: 999 rows remain instead of 857. Same with the vectorized and the row-based Spark reader.

Loading the delete file directly with BaseDeleteLoader.loadEqualityDeletes(...) returns a StructLikeSet of size 1, and set.contains(<one of the real keys>) is false.
Root cause

org.apache.iceberg.data.parquet.GenericParquetReaders$FixedReader.read(byte[] reuse) fills and returns the caller's reuse buffer (column.nextBinary().toByteBuffer().duplicate().get(reuse); return reuse;), so every record's fixed value is the same byte[] instance, mutated as the file is iterated.
BaseDeleteLoader.readEqDeletes passes the records (through a flyweight InternalRecordWrapper) to StructLikeSet.add, which goes through StructLikeWrapper.copyFor(s) -> set(s), which keeps only the StructLike reference and does not copy field values.

All N delete records end up aliasing one array, so after the file is read they all compare equal to the last value and the set collapses to one element. int/long/string keys are not affected because their values are fresh immutable objects per row; fixed (and any reused-buffer binary value) is.
Possible fix
Return a fresh array in FixedReader.read (or do not reuse for delete loading), or deep-copy field values when building the equality-delete StructLikeSet in readEqDeletes.
Found while building a native (vectorized) Iceberg scan for Spark that loads equality deletes through Iceberg's own loader; we now read the delete file ourselves and copy each key as it is read, which deletes the spec-correct rows.
Willingness to contribute

Apache Iceberg version: 1.12.0 (reproduced). The code involved appears unchanged on main (flink/v2.2), so the same behaviour is expected there.
Query engine: Flink (DynamicIcebergSink, DataStream API, upsert mode)
Please describe the bug 🐞
Summary
DynamicWriter and DynamicWriteResultAggregator cache per-table objects (task writer factories / manifest output file factories) that capture the Table loaded when the entry was created. The caches are keyed by table name (plus schema id / spec id for the writer), have no TTL and are never invalidated. When a table is dropped and re-created with the same name while the job is running, the cache key can match the old entry, so the sink keeps writing data files and manifests for the dropped table's location.
On Amazon S3 Tables this fails at the next checkpoint with AccessDeniedException (403) Could not access through this access point, because the dropped table's storage is no longer accessible. The TaskManager fails, the job restarts, the caches are rebuilt from scratch and the replayed records are written to the new table.
Root cause
Line numbers at tag apache-iceberg-1.12.0, flink/v2.2.

DynamicWriter#taskWriterFactories is an LRUCache<WriteTarget, RowDataTaskWriterFactory> (DynamicWriter.java:59,82). WriteTarget consists of table name, branch, schema id, spec id, upsert mode and equality fields (DynamicWriter.java:93-99), with no table identity such as the table UUID.
On a cache miss the factory loads the table once and captures it as () -> table (DynamicWriter.java:105-106,133-134). The writers map is cleared after every prepareCommit() (DynamicWriter.java:198), but the factories stay in the cache, so new writers in later checkpoints reuse the stale Table (location, FileIO).
DynamicWriteResultAggregator#outputFileFactoriesAndFormatVersions and #specs are LRUCaches keyed by table name only (DynamicWriteResultAggregator.java:71-72,99-100). outputFileFactoryAndFormatVersion() captures the loaded table the same way (DynamicWriteResultAggregator.java:210-230), so manifests are also created for the stale table.
TableMetadataCache (used by DynamicRecordProcessor) refreshes after cacheRefreshMs and sees the re-created table, so records reach the writer with the new table's schema id / spec id. A newly created table starts again at schema id 0 / spec id 0, which hits the stale WriteTarget entry.

Reproduction
DataStream job with DynamicIcebergSink (REST catalog on Amazon S3 Tables, upsert mode, equality field id, immediateTableUpdate(true)):

Write some rows to table db.t (schema (id INT PK, val STRING)) and let a checkpoint commit them.
Drop the table from the catalog (dropTable(db.t, purge=true)) while the job keeps running.
Write a row for db.t again, with the same or a different schema. The table is re-created (schema id 0, spec id 0).
At the next checkpoint:

Sink: Writer ... switched from RUNNING to FAILED
java.io.IOException: Could not perform checkpoint N for operator Sink: Writer
Caused by: java.io.IOException: software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.AccessDeniedException: Could not access through this access point (Service: S3, Status Code: 403, ...)
	at org.apache.iceberg.parquet.ParquetWriter.close(ParquetWriter.java:285)
	at org.apache.iceberg.io.DataWriter.close(DataWriter.java:83)
	at org.apache.iceberg.io.BaseTaskWriter$BaseRollingWriter.closeCurrent(BaseTaskWriter.java:435)
	...
	at org.apache.iceberg.flink.sink.UnpartitionedDeltaWriter.close(UnpartitionedDeltaWriter.java:69)
	at org.apache.iceberg.io.BaseTaskWriter.complete(BaseTaskWriter.java:148)

Expected: The sink writes to the re-created table.
Actual: The writer writes to the dropped table's location and the checkpoint fails. After the restart the job recovers, because the caches are empty.
Impact

On Amazon S3 Tables, every same-name drop + re-create causes one job failure / restart.
CDC pipelines that replicate DROP TABLE / CREATE TABLE (e.g. Debezium) hit this whenever a table is re-created with the same name. […]

Feature Request / Improvement
Vectorized Parquet reads in Spark support unshredded VARIANT columns (#16292), but not shredded ones.
Spark decides at planning time whether to read a scan vectorized. Whether a variant is shredded is only recorded in each data file's Parquet footer, so planning has to infer it from the table property, the column's metrics mode, and variant lower bounds. When that inference misses a shredded file, the vectorized read fails with UnsupportedOperationException: Unsupported variant: shredded typed_value ....
Reported failures:

#18430: a shredded variant is in the file but not projected.
#18601: a projected shredded variant has no variant bounds, for example when shredding was enabled through the session conf, or for shredded arrays.

Planning also sends any scan that projects a variant column to the row reader when the table sets the shred property or the column uses none/counts metrics, even if none of the files are shredded.
This issue tracks the work needed for Spark to read shredded variants vectorized without failing, and without relying on planning-time inference. Will update this issue as the PRs get added.

Apache Iceberg version
main (development)
Query engine
None
Please describe the bug 🐞
TableMetadata.Builder.removeSchemas filters schemas but leaves the removed ids in schemasById, and removeSpecs does the same with specsById. Later calls on the same builder still resolve the removed ids.
CatalogHandlers.commit applies every update in a request to one builder, so a transaction that expires unused metadata and then changes the schema hits this. Take a table whose current schema is 0 and whose schema 1 is unused because a column was added and then dropped:
table.updateSchema().addColumn("col_to_delete", Types.IntegerType.get()).commit();
table.updateSchema().deleteColumn("col_to_delete").commit();

Transaction transaction = table.newTransaction();
transaction.expireSnapshots().cleanExpiredMetadata(true).commit();
transaction.updateSchema().addColumn("new_col", Types.LongType.get()).commit();
transaction.commitTransaction();
The transaction sends remove-schemas [1], then add-schema for a new schema that the client assigned the freed id 1, then set-current-schema -1. On the server, addSchema finds id 1 in the stale index and does not add the new schema to schemas, and setCurrentSchema(1) picks up the removed schema instead. build() passes, and the server commits metadata with current-schema-id: 1 and only schema 0. The ops.current() call at the end of CatalogHandlers.commit then fails to read it back:
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Cannot find schema with current-schema-id=1 from schemas
	at org.apache.iceberg.TableMetadataParser.fromJson(TableMetadataParser.java:386)
	...
	at org.apache.iceberg.rest.CatalogHandlers.commit(CatalogHandlers.java:672)

The client sees a failed commit, but the metadata pointer has already moved, so every later loadTable fails with the same error.
The partition spec version (add a partition field and remove it, then cleanExpiredMetadata(true) and updateSpec().addField(...) in one transaction) is rejected instead. The new spec is skipped the same way, and set-default-spec -1 fails with Cannot set last added spec: no spec has been added.
InMemoryCatalog and JdbcCatalog are not affected, because BaseTransaction applies each operation to freshly built metadata. REST servers that commit through CatalogHandlers, or through their own copy of its commit loop, are affected.

body:
Feature Request / Improvement
Problem
UnboundPredicate.bindLiteralOperation folds a comparison whose literal converts to aboveMax() or belowMin() into alwaysTrue or alwaysFalse. That is exact for integers, but not on a float column: x < 1e100 binds to alwaysTrue, yet it is false for NaN and +Inf and unknown for null, and x > 1e100 binds to alwaysFalse although it is true for +Inf.
DoubleLiteral.to(FLOAT) also maps ±Infinity to aboveMax()/belowMin(), although infinity is a float value. On a float column, x = Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY and x >= Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY therefore bind to alwaysFalse and never match +Inf rows, and x <= Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY binds to alwaysTrue, which also matches NaN.
Proposal

Convert an infinite double to the float infinity in DoubleLiteral.to(FLOAT).
On a floating-point term, bind an ordering comparison against a finite out-of-range literal to a comparison against the largest finite value: x < 1e100 and x <= 1e100 become x <= Float.MAX_VALUE, x > 1e100 and x >= 1e100 become x > Float.MAX_VALUE, and the same below the minimum. Every float except +Inf lies below such a literal, so NaN, the infinities and null then compare as they do against the literal itself.

EQ and NOT_EQ can keep their folds.
Context
iceberg-go made this change in apache/iceberg-go#2355, so the two implementations now bind these filters differently.

body:
Feature Request / Improvement
Problem
Evaluator compares through literal comparators that order null first, so eq is false and notEq is true for a null value. in returns false for null, so notIn is true. Under SQL three-valued logic, x <> v and x NOT IN (...) are unknown when x is null, and a filter does not keep the row, so rows with a null value match notEq and notIn filters in Evaluator but not in SQL engines.
Proposal
Treat a comparison, in or notIn on a null value as unknown, and keep a row only when the filter is true, so that not of an unknown stays unknown. This would make Evaluator agree with SQL engines on null rows.
Open question
Whether Evaluator is meant to follow SQL semantics here, or is intentionally two-valued for callers that rely on the current behaviour.
Context
iceberg-go changed its row filter to SQL semantics for In and NotIn in apache/iceberg-go#2356; NotEqual already followed them.

Feature Request / Improvement
Iceberg writes spatial lower_bounds and upper_bounds for geometry columns in Parquet files. Add these metrics for spherical geography, per file and column. Longitude wraps at ±180°, and great circle edges can reach latitudes beyond their endpoints.
Split the work into steps:

Merge covered longitude intervals across the antimeridian. Bound memory use by widening intervals when needed.
Compute bounds for points and minor great circle edges, including latitude extrema and poles. Use world bounds for ambiguous edges.
Parse geography WKB and combine bounds per file and column. Use world bounds for nonempty polygons initially.
Write the metrics from generic and Spark Parquet writers.

Every box must cover all nonempty values in its column. Omit that column's bounds for the entire file if any value is malformed or unsupported, or if interpolation is unsupported. Keep existing count and size metrics. Initial scope is XY bounds; scan planning is separate work.
Tests should check coverage across the antimeridian, along curved edges, and after interval compaction. Writer tests should verify the recorded bounds, counts, and sizes.
Related: #17788 (closed, unmerged spherical bounds proposal), #17161 and #18501 (merged geometry support).

Feature Request / Improvement
Iceberg's Spark scan resolves the split target from the read option, session configuration, table property, or default, then may reduce it through adaptive sizing. The resulting target is passed to task-group planning, but the adjustment is currently visible only in a debug log. Scan analysis and autotuning tools cannot reliably recover the target from Spark SQL metrics or event logs. This matters when diagnosing scan partition sizes; see cudf-spark-tools#2206.
Please expose the effective split target size in bytes as a Spark scan driver metric, for example effectiveSplitTargetSize. Its value should be the target actually passed to task-group planning after configuration precedence and adaptive sizing are resolved, rather than an individual input partition's size.
Useful checks would cover an adaptive target, a configured target with adaptation disabled, an explicit read option, and staged rewrite scans that use their resolved target directly. An initial contribution can target Spark 4.2, with older Spark integrations considered separately.

Please describe the bug 🐞
When Write-Audit-Publish (WAP) is used via spark.wap.id on a format-version 3 table where deletion vectors (DVs) are in use, WAP snapshot isolation is broken in two related ways:
Failure mode 1 — WAP APPEND (INSERT):
Staged data becomes visible on the main branch before cherry-pick. Reading the table from the main branch after a WAP INSERT (without cherry-picking)
incorrectly returns the staged rows. Expected: main branch should not include any data from a staged WAP snapshot.
Failure mode 2 — WAP DELETE with write.delete.mode=merge-on-read:
The staged WAP snapshot does not appear in .snapshots filtered by its wap.id. SELECT snapshot_id FROM .snapshots WHERE summary['wap.id'] =
'' returns 0 rows, making any subsequent cherrypick_snapshot call impossible.
Steps to Reproduce
Using any Spark + Iceberg catalog (Hadoop, Hive, REST). Verified with Spark 3.5.x + Iceberg 1.10.1.
Failure mode (WAP DELETE):

USING iceberg
TBLPROPERTIES (
'format-version'       = '3',
'write.delete.mode'    = 'merge-on-read'
);
-- Step 2: Insert rows
INSERT INTO test_wap_dv
VALUES (1, 'Alice', 'Eng'), (2, 'Bob', 'HR'), (3, 'Carol', 'Eng');
-- Step 3: Enable WAP

SET TBLPROPERTIES ('write.wap.enabled' = 'true');

SET spark.wap.id = 'wap_stage_001';

body:
Apache Iceberg version
main (development)
Query engine
None
Please describe the bug 🐞
The expressions spec says float and double "use IEEE 754 order for all non-NaN values", and under that order -0.0 = 0.0. The wording was chosen on purpose in #16652 (discussion) to differ from IEEE total order, which puts -0.0 < 0.0. The Java evaluators use Comparator.naturalOrder() for float and double (Comparators.java), which is total order. So a row holding -0.0 doesn't match x = 0.0, and a data file or manifest whose only value is -0.0 gets pruned for x = 0.0, x IN (0.0, ...) and x >= 0.0.
Reproducer on main (be25281):
Schema schema = new Schema(Types.NestedField.required(1, "x", Types.DoubleType.get()));
Expression expr = Expressions.equal("x", 0.0);

new Evaluator(schema.asStruct(), expr).eval(TestHelpers.Row.of(-0.0)); // false, expected true

ByteBuffer negZero = Conversions.toByteBuffer(Types.DoubleType.get(), -0.0);
DataFile file =
    new TestHelpers.TestDataFile(
        "file.parquet", TestHelpers.Row.of(), 10,
        Map.of(1, 10L), Map.of(1, 0L), Map.of(1, 0L),
        Map.of(1, negZero), Map.of(1, negZero));
new InclusiveMetricsEvaluator(schema, expr).eval(file); // false (file skipped), expected true
ManifestEvaluator behaves the same way on an identity partition summary of [-0.0, -0.0].
Engines follow the spec here. Spark 3.5.3 and PostgreSQL 16 both evaluate CAST('-0.0' AS DOUBLE) = 0.0 as true and keep a -0.0 row for WHERE x = 0.0. If an engine pushes that filter down to Iceberg, files holding only -0.0 would be skipped and those rows lost. I haven't run that end to end with an Iceberg table.
Bounds are a separate rule: spec.md requires -0.0 to sort before +0.0 in lower/upper bounds, so Comparators can't simply switch to IEEE equality for everything. Where should the fix go: in the predicate comparisons only (Evaluator and the metrics/manifest evaluators), or somewhere else? I'm happy to work on it once the approach is agreed.
I used an AI assistant to help write the reproducer and checked the results and spec references myself.
